sourceEvidence.label: UX OS portal authentication, authorization, administration, and Canix access boundary

assessment.summary: The prepared capability model narrows inventory access, but privileged administration and its audit trail still need one server-owned transaction boundary.

nonNegotiables: Canix credentials and package rows must not enter the browser bundle.
Google authentication alone must never grant portal authorization.
External organization and location scope must remain enforced server-side.
assumptions: Supabase remains the identity, policy-data, and serverless execution platform for the next deployment phase.
No measured latency, memory, administration-volume, or audit-retention budget was supplied.
Existing internal users must not be locked out or silently promoted during the capability migration.

opportunities.title: Centralize privileged administration and audit
opportunities.summary: Make one server-owned authorization decision control every privileged mutation and append its audit record in the same transaction.
opportunities.diagnosis: The portal now has staff-role capabilities and a permission-aware inventory endpoint, but administrative mutations and audit behavior remain split between browser state, per-feature checks, and remote components whose source is not present locally.

evidence.claim: The client renders capability-filtered routes but models several user, role, impersonation, and audit operations in browser state.
The Canix endpoint independently checks inventory.read and inventory.sync before returning data or running a user-triggered sync.
A server-owned staff-role to permission mapping exists, but there is no common resource-aware authorization function or transactional admin RPC.
The existing private-table and service-role pattern can support a central privileged boundary without exposing operational tables to browser roles.

desiredInvariants: Every privileged portal mutation is authorized against the final user, capability, organization, location, and resource identity on the server.
The mutation and its security audit record either commit together or both fail.
A deactivated profile or removed grant takes effect at the next server request without relying on a refreshed browser menu.
External organization and location scope cannot be widened by request fields supplied by the browser.
The same capability names drive route discovery, endpoint enforcement, administration, and audit review.

options.title: Complete per-feature enforcement
options.summary: Keep each endpoint or RPC responsible for its own capability, scope, mutation, and audit checks while sharing the role-permission table.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: Server endpoints replace browser-only mutations, but callers can still drift in scope and audit behavior.
The inventory function already demonstrates this per-endpoint pattern.
Private tables remain behind service-owned operations.
The shared mapping reduces naming drift, but every caller still owns enforcement details.

tradeoffs.assessment: Browser-only privileged actions disappear, but future endpoints can still omit resource scope or audit writes.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Exercise every privileged endpoint with removed grants, cross-org identifiers, deactivated profiles, and missing audit writes.

tradeoffs.assessment: Checks remain inside the existing database or Edge Function request path and add no new network hop.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Compare p50 and p95 endpoint latency before and after capability and audit queries under representative admin traffic.

tradeoffs.assessment: The design adds only bounded permission and audit records to existing request processing.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Compare Edge Function peak memory for representative reads and writes.

tradeoffs.assessment: Server mutations become durable, but non-transactional feature implementations can still commit data without their audit event.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Inject audit-write and mutation failures into each endpoint and verify documented rollback behavior.

tradeoffs.assessment: Every feature team must maintain equivalent denial telemetry, audit fields, and incident queries.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Review the first three implemented endpoints for duplicated policy and alert definitions.

tradeoffs.assessment: Endpoints can move one at a time while the current UI remains available.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Migrate one low-risk admin action and confirm rollback requires only routing that action back to its prior disabled state.

residualRisks: Authorization, scope, and audit semantics can drift between endpoints.

acceptanceCriteria: No privileged state change succeeds without a server permission check and durable audit record.
migrationNotes: Migrate one action family at a time.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Disable the new action route and retain read-only administration while the endpoint is corrected.

options.title: Central Supabase policy and RPC boundary
options.summary: Use one resource-aware authorization function and transactional RPC boundary for privileged mutations and security audit writes.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: Browser actions become requests to server-owned RPCs; the client remains responsible only for presentation and denial recovery.
The inventory function can call the common decision function while keeping its existing token validation and private cache.
Security-definer RPCs extend the current private-table pattern without granting browser table access.
The existing capability vocabulary becomes the input to one owned, resource-aware decision point.

tradeoffs.assessment: Policy, resource scope, mutation, and audit commit behind one boundary, substantially reducing omission and drift paths.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run a deny matrix across role, capability, organization, location, resource alias, deactivation, and replay cases.

tradeoffs.assessment: Most decisions and writes stay within one Postgres transaction; Edge callers add a database RPC rather than another service hop.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure p50 and p95 RPC latency and set a release threshold no worse than the current endpoint plus one database round trip.

tradeoffs.assessment: Permission rows and bounded audit payloads add negligible request memory; audit storage growth is a disk-retention concern, not process memory.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure representative RPC response size and project audit-table growth from expected daily admin events.

tradeoffs.assessment: Transactional audit prevents successful mutations without their corresponding security event, while one database outage affects both consistently.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Force policy, mutation, and audit failures and verify atomic rollback plus stable error codes.

tradeoffs.assessment: One denial taxonomy, audit schema, and query surface simplify reviews, although the RPC layer becomes security-critical and needs ownership and change control.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Pilot alerting and quarterly access review queries against one migrated action family.

tradeoffs.assessment: Existing privileged flows must adopt typed RPC contracts and stable resource identities, but dual-read and action-by-action rollout remain possible.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Prototype user deactivation and staff-role assignment first, then estimate the remaining action families from the actual contract work.

residualRisks: A flaw in the central security-definer function affects every caller.
Audit retention, export, and independent tamper monitoring still require an explicit operations policy.

workPackages: Create portal_authorize and append-only audit schema
Adopt the decision function in Edge Functions
acceptanceCriteria: Every privileged mutation and audit record commit atomically after one resource-aware server decision.
migrationNotes: Seed existing internal users as viewers, explicitly bootstrap the first administrator, and verify every grant before release.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Disable migrated mutations and retain read-only administration; revert callers without removing the permission data or audit history.

options.title: Dedicated administration service
options.summary: Move privileged commands, policy decisions, and audit streaming into a separately deployed service with a command queue.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: The browser becomes an unprivileged client of a dedicated command API.
Inventory can remain a separate read service while admin-triggered sync commands enter the new boundary.
The service can retain private data ownership, but service credentials and network policy become new trusted components.
The capability mapping becomes policy input rather than caller-owned logic.

tradeoffs.assessment: Separate deployment and command isolation reduce browser and feature-service authority, but add service credentials, queue permissions, and network attack surface.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Threat-model service identity, queue tenancy, replay, confused-deputy, and break-glass paths before implementation.

tradeoffs.assessment: A network hop, serialization, and possible queue delay enter every privileged command.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Benchmark synchronous user and role changes plus queued long-running commands against product response targets.

tradeoffs.assessment: A separate runtime, queue buffers, worker concurrency, and audit stream retain more resources than an in-database transaction boundary.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure idle service memory, peak worker memory, and queue retention under burst scenarios.

tradeoffs.assessment: Failure isolation improves, but partial outages, retry semantics, poison commands, and queue backlogs create new recovery states.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run outage, duplicate-delivery, backpressure, and dead-letter recovery exercises before production cutover.

tradeoffs.assessment: The team must own another deployment, secret boundary, queue, dashboards, alerts, and incident playbook.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Estimate on-call and maintenance load from a service skeleton before committing.

tradeoffs.assessment: Every privileged action needs a command contract, idempotency key, worker, and dual-running plan.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Implement a non-production user-role command and use its measured engineering work to size the remaining migration.

residualRisks: Service credentials and queue permissions become high-value targets.
Eventual consistency can confuse administrators unless command status is explicit.
The operational burden may exceed current team capacity.

acceptanceCriteria: Privileged commands are authenticated, authorized, idempotent, auditable, and recoverable across service and queue failures.
migrationNotes: Run beside the Supabase path until command parity and recovery exercises pass.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Stop command intake and route unmigrated actions back to read-only or the prior Supabase boundary.

opportunities.recommendation: Use the central Supabase policy and RPC boundary while Supabase remains the portal platform; choose the dedicated service only if command volume, cross-system orchestration, or isolation requirements materially outgrow one database transaction boundary.

openQuestions: What retention period and independent export destination should apply to privileged security-audit events?
Which administrators may assign the administrator preset, and is two-person approval required for that elevation?
Which remote portal-intake operations currently mutate profiles or operational data, and can their source be brought into this repository?
